Well, honestly, doctor, I don't even know where to begin. I guess... well, I'm just completely falling apart. It really all started when those foreclosure notices started coming in the mail. I mean, they just keep arriving, and every time I see one, or even think about the mail, my stomach just drops. It’s like this heavy, sick feeling that I can’t shake. 

Ever since those letters started showing up, I just feel like I’m coming apart at the seams. I’m a heavy equipment mechanic, right? I work on massive diesel rigs, excavators, loaders... it’s a tough environment, you gotta be thick-skinned and focused. But lately? I’m sitting out in my pickup in the shop parking lot before my shift, just bawling my eyes out. Just crying over the steering wheel, trying to get it together for twenty minutes before I finally force myself to clock in. 

And if my cell phone rings? I practically jump out of my skin. I just flinch and my heart starts pounding because I'm terrified it's the bank calling again. And it’s spilling over into my work, which is what really scares me. I’m snapping at the young apprentices over every little thing—if they hand me a 3/8ths instead of a half-inch drive, I just bite their heads off, which isn't fair to them at all. And worse, I'm making mistakes. Stupid, careless mistakes in the repair bay. Things I have never, ever made in my entire career turning wrenches, like forgetting to double-check a high-pressure fitting. I just... I can't keep it together anymore, and I don't know how to fix it.

Well, no, I wouldn't say it's a sudden thing that just peaks out of nowhere, if that's what you mean. It's not like a lightning bolt of fear. It’s... well, it’s more like this constant, heavy, grinding dread that just never really leaves me alone.

So, no, it's not a sudden attack of fear that comes and goes. It's just always, always there. It's just sitting right on my chest, weighing me down while I'm trying to wrench on these rigs and keep my head straight for ten hours a day.

I look at my friends in the truck club, and they're all doing fine. They're upgrading their suspensions, putting new crate motors in their C10s, and I'm just... I'm a complete failure. I feel like I've let myself down, I've let my parents down—God rest their souls, they'd be so ashamed if they saw me right now, facing foreclosure. It's just this overwhelming sense of guilt that I ruined my own life, and I don't even know how to fix it. Anxious most of the time? Even when nothing is happening? Um... no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, don't get me wrong, I'm a mess about the house and the bank and work, but... it's not like I'm just sitting around terrified of, I don't know, the sky falling or something. My heart wasn't racing. I was just looking at a box that said "Fleetguard FS1000" and making sure it went in the right bin. I wasn't worried about anything else in the world except those filters. And sometimes, if I'm driving home and a really good song comes on the radio—like old Bob Seger or something—I can just listen to the music and watch the road, and I don't feel that tight knot in my stomach. 

So, no, it's not this constant, free-floating panic all day long. It's very specifically tied to the mess I'm in. When the mail comes, or when I look at my toolbox, or when I'm alone in the quiet like I said before... that's when it hits me like a ton of bricks. But if I can manage to distract myself, or if there's literally nothing going on to trigger it, I don't feel that anxiousness. It's really just the reality of my situation that's causing it, not some random fear out of nowhere. If I could just fix the money issue, I know I'd be perfectly fine.

Sad? Depressed? I mean... I don't think I'd use those words. When I think of somebody who's depressed, I picture someone who just lays in bed all day in the dark, crying, and can't even, you know, find the will to put their boots on. That's not me at all.

It’s like this heavy, sick feeling that I can’t shake. \n\nEver since those letters started showing up, I just feel like I’m coming apart at the seams. I’m a heavy equipment mechanic, right? I’m sitting out in my pickup in the shop parking lot before my shift, just bawling my eyes out. I just flinch and my heart starts pounding because I'm terrified it's the bank calling again. And it’s spilling over into my work, which is what really scares me. I’m snapping at the young apprentices over every little thing—if they hand me a 3/8ths instead of a half-inch drive, I just bite their heads off, which isn't fair to them at all. And worse, I'm making mistakes. Stupid, careless mistakes in the repair bay. Things I have never, ever made in my entire career turning wrenches, like forgetting to double-check a high-pressure fitting. I just... I can't keep it together anymore, and I don't know how to fix it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a sudden feeling of intense fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I wouldn't say it's a sudden thing that just peaks out of nowhere, if that's what you mean. It's not like a lightning bolt of fear. It’s... well, it’s more like this constant, heavy, grinding dread that just never really leaves me alone. \n\nLike I mentioned with the cell phone ringing—sure, I jump, and my heart does a little tap dance because I'm scared it's a debt collector, but it doesn't build up into this huge, overwhelming peak of terror for minutes on end. It’s just a quick jolt, and then I'm right back to that same low, sick feeling in my gut that I've had all day. I mean, from the second my alarm goes off at 4:30 in the morning and I'm lacing up my steel-toes, I'm already chewing on it. I'm thinking about the mortgage, I'm wondering where in the world I'm going to put all my heavy Snap-on toolboxes if the bank actually takes the house, how I'm going to explain it to people... \n\nSo, no, it's not a sudden attack of fear that comes and goes. It's just always, always there. It's just sitting right on my chest, weighing me down while I'm trying to wrench on these rigs and keep my head straight for ten hours a day.\n\nDoctor: Have you been avoiding social situations or gatherings because of your current state?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. I mean, it's just completely taken over everything. It’s funny you ask that, because I used to be so involved in things, you know? Like, I’ve always been the type to keep busy. But now? I just... My supervisor, Dave, pulled me aside last Tuesday... or maybe it was Wednesday? But it's humiliating. I'm practically doing lube-tech work now, sweeping up and organizing parts bins. \n\nAnd outside of the shop? Forget about it. I used to volunteer at my church every other Sunday, helping run the food pantry. I haven't been in a month. I just can't face those people, you know? They’re all so nice and they always ask how I’m doing, and I know if I try to answer, I’ll just start crying right there in the fellowship hall. I also stopped going to my Wednesday night Zumba fitness classes. I used to love those—it was a great way to sweat out the grease and grime from the week, but now I just drive straight home, lock the door, and stare at the wall. \n\nEven my truck club... I have this group of friends, we all have classic Chevy C10s, and we usually do a cruise-in at the Sonic over on Route 9 every first Saturday of the month. It's like a snowball rolling downhill, just getting bigger and heavier. And I sit there and my chest gets tight, and my stomach is just tied in these awful knots, and I can't stop it. I try to tell myself to just breathe, or to go make some tea or something, but I just end up frozen there on the couch for hours, just trapped in my own head with all these terrible scenarios playing out like a movie I can't turn off. I don't know, my eating habits seem pretty much the same. And for dinner, well, I still manage to throw something together, even if it's just heating up a can of soup or making some mac and cheese. I don't really have the energy to cook a big meal, but I'm still eating my normal amounts, I suppose. I haven't lost or gained any weight that I can tell. It's just this overwhelming sense of guilt that I ruined my own life, and I don't even know how to fix it. Even when nothing is happening? Um... no, I wouldn't really say that. If there's no reason to be anxious right in front of me, or if my brain isn't actively chewing on the foreclosure, I can actually feel somewhat normal for a minute. \n\nLike yesterday, for example. I was at the shop, and Dave had me reorganizing the entire back stockroom. My heart wasn't racing. I was just looking at a box that said \"Fleetguard FS1000\" and making sure it went in the right bin. I wasn't worried about anything else in the world except those filters. Oh, absolutely not. If you took away the bank and the shop mess, I'd be my old self in a heartbeat. I can trace it exactly back to when those foreclosure notices started showing up in the mail. Before that, I was rock solid. But ever since that first certified letter arrived... I just feel like I’m completely coming apart at the seams. It's like my whole system is just overloaded and I can't handle basic things anymore. 

Take my mornings, for instance. I used to just grab my coffee, listen to the morning show on the radio, and head in, ready to tackle a transmission rebuild or whatever was on the board. Now? I pull into the shop parking lot, sit in my truck with the engine running, and I just start crying. I don't even want to, the tears just come out of nowhere. I have to sit there wiping my eyes with a fast-food napkin for ten minutes before I can even pull myself together enough to walk through the bay doors. 

And my nerves are just completely shot all day long. Every single time the phone rings—whether it's my cell buzzing in my pocket or the loud ringer on the landline over by the parts desk—I literally jump. My shoulders hit my ears because I'm terrified it's a debt collector calling again, or Dave calling me into the front office to tell me he's letting me go completely. 

It's even bleeding into how I treat people, which I really hate. We have these two new apprentices at the shop, young kids, maybe 19 or 20, fresh out of diesel tech school. Normally I have a lot of patience for the greenhorns, you know? I like showing them the right way to bleed a brake line on a Peterbilt or how to properly pack a bearing. But lately? I'm snapping at them over the absolute smallest things. Like, if one of them hands me a 9/16 wrench when I clearly asked for a half-inch, I just bite their head off. I yelled at one of the kids so loud on Tuesday that the air compressors were running and people still turned around to look. 

But the worst part... the absolute worst part, and the thing that really scares me, is that I'm making stupid mistakes in the repair bay. Mistakes I never, ever would have made before all this started. I've been turning wrenches for over twenty years! But just last week, I completely forgot to torque the lug nuts on a dual-wheel axle. I just... I got distracted thinking about the mortgage, and I walked right past it. Thank God Dave was doing a final walk-around and caught it before the rig rolled out, because if that wheel had come off on the highway, it could have killed somebody. I felt sick to my stomach for two days over it. So, yeah, if the foreclosure and the work stuff were gone, none of this would be happening. I wouldn't be acting like this. It's 100 percent because of the mess I'm in.

When I'm just sitting there by myself. I mean, at work, even though I'm just organizing parts bins and sweeping up right now, at least my hands are moving, you know? At least I have to focus on putting the 10-millimeter sockets in the right drawer and not mixing up the O-rings. But when I go home... it's just me. I live alone, well, just me and my cat, Buster, but he's not exactly a great conversationalist. \n\nSo I get home, I lock the door, and the house is just so quiet. And that's when my brain just starts going a million miles an hour. I'll sit down on the couch—I don't even turn the TV on anymore, I just sit there—and the thoughts just start piling up on top of each other. I start thinking about the bank, and then I think about the letters, and then I start picturing them coming to change the locks. I imagine where I'm going to sleep. I think about my tools, my big roll-cab toolbox that I've been paying off for five years... how am I going to move it? Where does it go if I don't have a garage? \n\nIt just spirals. It's like a snowball rolling downhill, just getting bigger and heavier. And I sit there and my chest gets tight, and my stomach is just tied in these awful knots, and I can't stop it. I try to tell myself to just breathe, or to go make some tea or something, but I just end up frozen there on the couch for hours, just trapped in my own head with all these terrible scenarios playing out like a movie I can't turn off. So, yeah, being alone with my thoughts... it's honestly the most agonizing part of my entire day. I almost dread going home because I know what's waiting for me in the quiet.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing any changes in your appetite or sleep patterns lately?\n\nPatient: Well, as far as changes in my appetite or sleep... I mean, I guess I haven't really noticed anything major with either of those. It's funny, because you'd think with all this stress, I'd be stress-eating or not sleeping a wink, but... I don't know, my eating habits seem pretty much the same. I still pack my lunch for work every day—usually just a turkey sandwich, maybe some pretzels, an apple if I remember to grab one from the bowl on the counter. And for dinner, well, I still manage to throw something together, even if it's just heating up a can of soup or making some mac and cheese. I don't really have the energy to cook a big meal, but I'm still eating my normal amounts, I suppose. I haven't lost or gained any weight that I can tell. It's just... everything else that feels like it's falling apart.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty or worthless about your current situation?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Worthless? Oh, God, yes. I keep thinking I should have been smarter. I should have seen this coming. I feel so incredibly stupid. And worthless? Yeah, absolutely. When Dave pulled me off the high-risk bay... I mean, I know he was doing it for safety, I know I was messing up, but it just completely broke me. My job, being a mechanic, fixing things that are broken... that's who I am. That's my identity. They're upgrading their suspensions, putting new crate motors in their C10s, and I'm just... I'm a complete failure. I feel like I've let myself down, I've let my parents down—God rest their souls, they'd be so ashamed if they saw me right now, facing foreclosure. It's just this overwhelming sense of guilt that I ruined my own life, and I don't even know how to fix it. I can fix a blown transmission, but I can't fix this, and it makes me feel like I'm just completely useless.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious most of the time, even when there's no immediate threat or stressor?\n\nPatient: Anxious most of the time? Even when nothing is happening? Um... no, I wouldn't really say that. It's like a black hole right in the middle of my life, sucking all my attention and energy into it. It's right there, all the time.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel sad or depressed most of the time?\n\nPatient: Sad? Depressed? I mean... I don't think I'd use those words. Oh, God, yes. Yes, I really do. If I could just wake up tomorrow and the bank called to say, "Hey, we worked it out, your house is safe," or if Dave came up to me and said, "You're back on the heavy repairs full-time, don't worry about it," I swear to you, this whole nightmare in my head would just evaporate. There hasn't been any sort of finish line for my brain to even try and recover from, you know what I mean? It's like... you can't heal a burn while your hand is still pressed flat against the hot exhaust manifold. And my hand is definitely still on the manifold. If it was over, if it was all fixed and in the rearview mirror, I know I'd be fine. I'd go back to just being me, turning wrenches and going home to a house that's actually mine. But right now, with the deadlines still looming and the phone still ringing... it's just not over, so the panic isn't over either.

I used to love those—it was a great way to sweat out the grease and grime from the week, but now I just drive straight home, lock the door, and stare at the wall. \n\nEven my truck club... I have this group of friends, we all have classic Chevy C10s, and we usually do a cruise-in at the Sonic over on Route 9 every first Saturday of the month. We pop the hoods, talk shop, grab a burger... I haven't shown my face there since the first foreclosure notice arrived. I just keep making up excuses. I tell them I'm waiting on parts, or I have a migraine, but the truth is, I just can't stomach the idea of standing around making small talk and pretending everything is fine when I feel like my whole life is literally being repossessed. I just don't want to be around anyone. It's too exhausting to pretend.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you're alone with your thoughts?\n\nPatient: Oh, well, that's... yeah, that's really when it gets the worst, to be honest. When I'm just sitting there by myself. I mean, at work, even though I'm just organizing parts bins and sweeping up right now, at least my hands are moving, you know? At least I have to focus on putting the 10-millimeter sockets in the right drawer and not mixing up the O-rings. But when I go home... it's just me. I live alone, well, just me and my cat, Buster, but he's not exactly a great conversationalist. \n\nSo I get home, I lock the door, and the house is just so quiet. And that's when my brain just starts going a million miles an hour. I'll sit down on the couch—I don't even turn the TV on anymore, I just sit there—and the thoughts just start piling up on top of each other. I start thinking about the bank, and then I think about the letters, and then I start picturing them coming to change the locks. I imagine where I'm going to sleep. I think about my tools, my big roll-cab toolbox that I've been paying off for five years... how am I going to move it? Where does it go if I don't have a garage? \n\nIt just spirals. It's like a snowball rolling downhill, just getting bigger and heavier. And I sit there and my chest gets tight, and my stomach is just tied in these awful knots, and I can't stop it. I try to tell myself to just breathe, or to go make some tea or something, but I just end up frozen there on the couch for hours, just trapped in my own head with all these terrible scenarios playing out like a movie I can't turn off. So, yeah, being alone with my thoughts... it's honestly the most agonizing part of my entire day. I almost dread going home because I know what's waiting for me in the quiet.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing any changes in your appetite or sleep patterns lately?\n\nPatient: Well, as far as changes in my appetite or sleep... I mean, I guess I haven't really noticed anything major with either of those. It's funny, because you'd think with all this stress, I'd be stress-eating or not sleeping a wink, but... I don't know, my eating habits seem pretty much the same. I still pack my lunch for work every day—usually just a turkey sandwich, maybe some pretzels, an apple if I remember to grab one from the bowl on the counter. I don't really have the energy to cook a big meal, but I'm still eating my normal amounts, I suppose. I haven't lost or gained any weight that I can tell. Buster sometimes jumps on the bed and wakes me up, but that's been happening for years. So, yeah, I wouldn't say my sleep or my appetite have really changed. It's just... everything else that feels like it's falling apart.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty or worthless about your current situation?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Worthless? Oh, God, yes. All the time. I mean, it's just this constant, heavy feeling sitting right on my chest. It's like... how did I let this happen, you know? I'm 47 years old. I've been working since I was 16. I keep thinking I should have been smarter. I should have seen this coming. I feel so incredibly stupid. And worthless? Yeah, absolutely. When Dave pulled me off the high-risk bay... I mean, I know he was doing it for safety, I know I was messing up, but it just completely broke me. My job, being a mechanic, fixing things that are broken... that's who I am. That's my identity. It's just this overwhelming sense of guilt that I ruined my own life, and I don't even know how to fix it. I can fix a blown transmission, but I can't fix this, and it makes me feel like I'm just completely useless.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious most of the time, even when there's no immediate threat or stressor?\n\nPatient: Anxious most of the time? It's really just the reality of my situation that's causing it, not some random fear out of nowhere. It's like my head is just a one-track mind, and that track is heading straight for a cliff. \n\nI don't really worry about my health or anything like that. It's like a black hole right in the middle of my life, sucking all my attention and energy into it. I want my bay back, I want my life back, and I'm just mad that I screwed it all up. But sad? No, I really don't think that's the right word for it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would feel anxious if you weren't dealing with the foreclosure and work issues?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely not. It's very specifically tied to the mess I'm in. When the mail comes, or when I look at my toolbox, or when I'm alone in the quiet like I said before... that's when it hits me like a ton of bricks. It's really just the reality of my situation that's causing it, not some random fear out of nowhere. And my friends in the truck club, they're all doing fine. Better than fine, actually. They've got their lives together. So I don't fret over them. Really, it's just this one massive, overwhelming thing. The foreclosure, the bank, Dave pulling me off the floor... it just consumes everything. It's like a black hole right in the middle of my life, sucking all my attention and energy into it. So, yeah, if you take away the financial mess and the work stuff, I don't think I'd have a single care in the world. But unfortunately, I can't just take it away, can I? Doc, I feel like we're kind of going in circles here, because... well, no. I really, truly wouldn't. Like I was saying a few minutes ago, if there's no major stressor—if the engine isn't actively on fire—I'm not going to sit around sweating about whether it *might* catch fire someday. I've got 47 years of evidence proving I don't do that. Back before all this mess started, before Dave started breathing down my neck at the shop and the bank started hounding me, my days were just... they were peaceful. I'd do my job, wash the grease off my hands with that gritty orange pumice soap, and come home. And once I was home, my brain was completely off the clock. 

I wasn't pacing the floors wondering if the water heater was going to break, or if the grocery store was going to run out of my favorite coffee, or what somebody meant when they said hello to me weird. I'd just sit on the porch, maybe have a beer, watch the neighbor's dog chase squirrels, and that was it. My mind was quiet. I don't have this... this built-in need to find things to panic about. 

I really think some people are just born with their idle set too high, you know? Like my sister, like I mentioned. Her brain is just constantly revving, constantly looking for a problem to latch onto even when everything is perfectly fine. But my idle has always been set perfectly low. If there's nothing broken, I don't go looking for something to fix. So no, if you take away the actual, real-life disasters happening to me right now, I wouldn't be worrying to the point of feeling like this. I just wouldn't. I'd go right back to being the exact same person I was before the mail carrier started bringing me certified letters.
